A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Importance Corrected Neural JKO Sampling by the same authors. Their readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including Appendices A–E in v1 and A–F in v2.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original sampling experiments, including energy distances, log-normalizer estimates, mode-weight errors, and comparisons with uncorrected neural JKO.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds Wasserstein evaluations, GMM40-50D results, and trained normalizing-flow comparisons. Some comparator scores are explicitly borrowed, but original results are clearly present.

M1.justification: The core CNF and rejection-resampling procedure remains. Remark E.2 adds a fixed score-gradient flow initialization before learned steps for GMM40-50D. Remark F.3 also outlines an adaptation to other flow architectures using a squared-displacement penalty.

E1.justification: The original target distributions remain, including LGCP. Appendix E.1 adds GMM40-50D, a 50-dimensional mixture with 40 modes, identity covariances, and means drawn from [-40,40]^d. This extends the represented multimodal sampling scenarios beyond the retained ten-mode GMM family.

E2.justification: The original comparator set is retained. New Table 5 adds SMC, PIS, CMCD-LV, and SCLD, using comparison scores attributed to Chen et al. (2025). Appendix F.3 and Table 7 additionally evaluate standard continuous and Glow-coupling normalizing flows, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds empirical squared Wasserstein-2 evaluation using 5,000 samples and a Sinkhorn protocol using 2,000 samples with regularization 10^-3. It also introduces standalone-flow comparison configurations and GMM40-50D settings, including latent scaling 40 and initialization time 3. The original 50,000-sample energy, log-normalizer, and mode-weight evaluations remain.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds substantive mode-collapse analyses: Example F.1 and Figure 12 examine a nonconvex loss landscape, while F.3 and Figure 13 examine collapse in standard continuous and coupling flows across several targets. These complement the retained rejection-step ablation and layerwise diagnostics.

E5.justification: The existing five-run mean and standard-deviation reporting remains. The new GMM40-50D experiment specifies five training runs with 25 evaluations per run and reuse of the benchmark's mode-generation seed. New Table 7 reports point estimates without uncertainty information; no increase in repetitions for the retained experiments is established.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results as v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4. v2 adds extensive results in Tables 3, 5, and 7 and revises layerwise error curves. For example, new Table 5 reports Sinkhorn distance 3025.61 ± 418.10 for neural JKO IC versus 3787.73 ± 249.75 for SCLD on the added benchmark.

T1.justification: The central convergence and KL-decrease guarantees remain. Section 3 and Appendix B.1 correct the reverse-KL condition from lambda-convexity of q to lambda-convexity of -log(q). Appendix C.1 replaces point-probability reasoning with a measurable-set density proof, and Example F.1 adds a formal mode-collapse construction.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and methodological conclusion retain the same central claims: combining neural JKO with importance-based rejection, generating independent samples with evaluable densities, velocity-field convergence, decreasing reverse KL, and strong sampling performance up to dimension 1600.

C2.justification: Appendix F substantially expands explanations of mode collapse, Wasserstein regularization, and computational tradeoffs involving ODE differentiation, trace estimation, and alternative architectures. Appendix E.2 adds concrete limitations of empirical Wasserstein evaluation in high dimensions. F.3 also introduces an overbroad 'always better' interpretation despite Table 7's Funnel energy-distance exception.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's architecture, timing, hardware, and code information, v2 documents batch sizes and GPU memory, the 50,000-sample training buffer and refresh procedure, adjoint differentiation with dopri5, zero initialization, and training versus evaluation trace-sample counts. It also supplies new benchmark and comparator configurations. Much of this is newly disclosed detail, not evidence of changed retained experiments.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands its positioning: distinguishing generative modeling from density-based sampling, contrasting SMC density approximations and sampling costs, and discussing flow matching, flow-assisted MCMC, and birth-death methods. It adds relevant works such as Marzouk et al., Gabrié et al., and Chen et al., alongside related preprints released after v1.

P1.justification: The six main sections and much of the original narrative remain. v2 rewrites related work and selected explanations, moves the outline before related work, introduces additional appendix subsections and an impact statement, and updates terminology, affiliations, and headings. Rewriting is concentrated in these portions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, moves rejection pseudocode into the main text, and adds an overall algorithm display. It adds Tables 3, 5, and 7 and Figures 2, 12, and 13, expands the implementation table, and redraws retained plots with different colors and sizing. Original Figures 2–10 correspond to Figures 3–11.

improvement.justification: The added standard-flow controls, broader sampling comparisons, implementation disclosures, and repaired density proof make the paper easier to assess and reproduce. These gains are tempered by missing uncertainty information in Table 7 and overstated interpretation in F.3: coupling NF has better Funnel energy distance, 2.2×10^-3 versus 1.4×10^-2, despite the 'always better' claim. The net improvement is useful but limited.
